Source-Modality Monitoring in Vision-Language Models

Etha Tianze Hua    Tian Yun    Ellie Pavlick Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, Brown University Email: {tianze_hua,tian_yun,ellie_pavlick}@brown.edu
Abstract

We define and investigate source-modality monitoring–the ability of multimodal models to track and communicate the input source from which pieces of information originate. We consider source-modality monitoring as an instance of the more general binding problem, and evaluate the extent to which models exploit syntactic vs. semantic signals in order to bind words like image in a user-provided prompt to specific components of their input and context (i.e., actual images). Across experiments spanning 11 vision-language models (VLMs) performing target-modality information retrieval tasks, we find that both syntactic and semantic signals play an important role, but that the latter tend to outweigh the former in cases when modalities are highly distinct distributionally. We discuss the implications of these findings for model robustness, and in the context of increasingly multimodal agentic systems.11 1 All resources will be available at https://github.com/ethahtz/source-modality-monitoring.

1 Introduction

We are moving toward a world of multimodal AI agents that must build and update world models from many sources of information and interaction (Li et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025; Fung et al., 2025; Team et al., 2025a). In order for humans to interact effectively with such systems, AI models need to be able to track and communicate where (i.e., from which modality) information comes from. Borrowing terminology from cognitive psychology (Johnson et al., 1993; Henkel et al., 2000), we refer to this ability as source-modality monitoring.

We consider source-modality monitoring as an instance of the more general binding problem (Smolensky, 1990): a model must associate particular content with an abstract role, such as image or text, and retrieve the content corresponding to the queried role. Recent work has shown that language models solve related binding problems through abstract, symbolic-like mechanisms, for example by associating entities with their attributes (Feng and Steinhardt, 2024; Gur-Arieh et al., 2025) or binding values to variables (Wu et al., 2025). Given this, we might expect modern multimodal models to invoke a similar mechanism for binding inputs to modalities, especially since their inputs are often explicitly marked with modality-specific wrapper tokens such as <image> and </image>.

However, viewing source-modality monitoring as a case of purely symbolic binding misses many of the key properties. Namely, unlike arbitrary role labels, words such as image and text are grounded in content with distinct distributional and semantic structure. Some kinds of inputs just are images, regardless of whether or not they are tagged as such. As a result, when a multimodal model is asked to report “what is in the image,” it need not rely only on explicit modality markers; it should also be able to infer from the nature of the input itself whether or not a piece of information should bind to a word like image. Moreover, as AI becomes increasingly multimodal and agentic, it becomes unrealistic to assume that all the “modalities” to which a human might refer will be explicitly tagged. Humans might ask AI for information from “yesterday’s meeting”, or “the discussion about dinner plans”. In such cases, AI will need to rely on contextual and distributional information about the content being bound, instead or in addition to information available in explicit syntactic markers.

In this paper, we ask if and how modern vision-language models (VLMs) accomplish source-modality monitoring. Source-modality monitoring can be studied at multiple levels, including mechanisms acquired over training (Khalifa et al., 2024) and mechanisms deployed in context at inference time. We focus on the latter, and investigate how it is accomplished in a variety of VLMs across model sizes and preprocessing choices. We first show that many of these models perform well on a task designed to test in-context source-modality monitoring, and that models with explicit marker tokens (e.g., <image>&</image>) generally outperform those without them. We then ask what kind of signal supports this performance. By structurally perturbing symbolic modality markers, we find that models’ binding behavior is driven primarily by distributional semantic signals rather than purely symbolic ones, although explicit markers still improve selectivity. Finally, by applying optimized transformations to marker and content representations, we show that symbolic cues can nonetheless be exploited to reverse models’ modality attribution. Together, these results provide a more nuanced picture of how syntactic and semantic signals combine to support binding in complex multimodal settings.

2 How Well Do VLMs Bind Words to Their Inputs?

2.1 Target-Modality Retrieval Task

We first ask simply whether VLMs are capable of associating different parts of their input (i.e., images, text) with the words that refer to those inputs (image, caption)? We define the following task whose successful performance depends on a model’s ability to monitor source modality. Each instance consists of a single in-context inconsistent image-caption pair, and the model is prompted to retrieve information from one specified input source (e.g., “what is in the image” or “what is in the caption”). We refer to the queried source as the target modality and the other source as the non-target modality. Figure 1 shows an example, illustrating the correct answers when a model is asked to retrieve image or caption information from its input pair. We exclude the possibility that VLMs rely on input order to retrieve information by evaluating them under both input orderings -- image tokens first or text tokens first -- and report the average result across the two conditions.22 2 We adapt this approach to all models except InstructBLIP, which has a fixed order of having image tokens at the beginning of the input sequence.

Because the visual and textual inputs convey mutually exclusive information, answering correctly requires the model to retrieve content from the specified target modality. As the target modality is explicitly indicated, this task does not merely measure a model’s overall modality bias, but instead targets at the model’s ability to associate retrieved information with its input modality thus making it suitable for assessing source-modality monitoring.

2.2 Datasets and Models

To construct inconsistent image–caption pairs, we leverage existing image captioning datasets flickr30k (Young et al., 2014) and MSCOCO (Lin et al., 2015), and systematically sample captions that are inconsistent with the visual content of each image. We use a simple heuristic procedure to ensure that the caption paired with the image is genuinely mismatched at the semantic level. To do this, we require that the sampled caption have cosine similarity below a threshold of 0.20.2 with any of the five image’s ground-truth associated captions, where similarity is computed using a BERT-style sentence embedding model (sentence-transformers/all-mpnet-base-v2 (Song et al., 2020)).

We evaluate a range of 11 open-source VLMs on this task. Beyond differences in model size, these systems also vary along an architectural dimension that is especially relevant to our setting: whether the input preprocessing pipeline inserts explicit image wrapper tokens that mark the span of image tokens. Qwen-2.5-VL, InternVL3, and Gemma-3 models(Bai et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025; Team et al., 2025b) are trained with these wrapper tokens, while earlier models such as LLaVA-1.5(Liu et al., 2023), InstructBLIP(Dai et al., 2023), and LLaVA-OneVision(Li et al., 2025) do not use such markers. See Table 3 for the image marker tokens used across model families. This variation allows us to ask whether the presence of modality-marking tokens is associated with stronger retrieval from the target modality.

2.3 Metrics and Baselines

Metrics

To measure how reliably models retrieve information from the target modality, we first identify valid predictions, namely outputs that clearly report information from either the target modality or the non-target modality (i.e., as opposed to outputting nonsense, which models sometimes do). Then, we define selectivity as an aggregate metric which indicates the tendency of the model to return the modality that was requested in the prompt. To obtain selectivity, we compute the difference between the frequency with which the model reports information from the target modality and the frequency with which it reports information from the non-target modality, among these valid predictions.33 3 See Appendix B for the formal definitions of valid prediction rate and selectivity. This yields a score in the range [−1,1][-1,1]: a score of 11 indicates perfect retrieval from the target modality, a score of 00 indicates no preference between the two modalities, and a score of −1-1 indicates that the model always retrieves information from the non-target modality instead.

Since we construct our input pairs from captioning datasets, model outputs are often free-form and cannot be evaluated with exact string matching. We therefore use GPT5.4-mini (OpenAI, 2026) as an LLM judge to evaluate whether model outputs are grounded in the image, the caption, or neither. We include examples of model outputs and judged outcomes in Appendix G.

Single-Modality Baseline

To contextualize the rate of valid responses under the inconsistent two-modality input pairs, we include a single-modality baseline in which a model receives input from only one modality and is prompted to report information from that modality. We use the same GPT model as the LLM Judge to evaluate whether the response sufficiently reports what is in its input.

2.4 Results

Valid Responses

Figure 2 shows the valid-response rates and selectivity scores for all 11 models in our evaluation. With the exception of InstructBLIP-7B, most models maintain a near-perfect valid-response rate under inconsistent inputs, in some cases even exceeding their single-modality baselines. One possible explanation is that inconsistent inputs encourage models to give more specific responses about the queried target modality, yielding slightly higher valid-response rates than in the single-modality setting. Still, the difference is small, suggesting that these models can report information from at least one modality with a level of specificity comparable to that seen when only a single modality is provided.

Modality Selectivity

All models, except for InstructBLIP-7B, outperform the random baseline in selectivity, indicating that they retrieve information from the target modality more often than from the non-target modality. That said, there is substantial variation between models, and many smaller models struggle to reliably return the requested information. InstructBLIP-7B shows an interesting negative selectivity, indicating it more frequently reports information from the non-target modality than the target modality. Conceptually, the worst performing model would be at chance level – we suspect InstructBLIP is below chance level because of its fixed-order design, which puts the image tokens always before the textual tokens, that lead to a constant bias which leads to the negative selectivity. On the other end, models such as Gemma-3-12B and Qwen2.5-VL-32B perform nearly perfectly, almost achieving the ceiling performance. In general, larger models tend to perform better than smaller models; but we also observe that models with special image wrapper tokens (marked with ★\bigstar in the figure) outperform models without such tokens. We explore this mechanism in detail in subsequent sections.

3 Role of Symbolic vs. Distributional Signals in Word-Input Binding

The strong performance of VLMs which have special image wrapper tokens on the target-modality retrieval task might suggest that source-modality monitoring is driven primarily by these symbolic marker tokens. This would resemble the largely symbolic binding mechanisms previously studied in language models, such as binding entities to their attributes (Feng and Steinhardt, 2024; Gur-Arieh et al., 2025). In this section, however, we show a more nuanced picture. First, we show that VLMs are indeed capable of solving a purely symbolic binding problem when there is no distributional signal to exploit. Second, we confirm that image and text content tokens differ markedly in their representations’ distributions, providing an additional/alternative cue for modality identity. Third, we show that source-modality monitoring is a hybrid syntactic-semantic mechanism: models rely in part on distributional content cues to guide retrieval, but symbolic markers help contextualize content tokens, leading to a more robust encoding of modality identity. We focus our analysis on three best-performing models from different model families from the previous section.

3.1 VLMs Are Capable of Symbolic Binding

We begin by asking whether models can use symbols as pure indexing devices. To isolate this capacity, we test VLMs with a simpler symbolic binding task in which the two input sources are labeled by arbitrary labels such as Alpha and Beta or Dax and Wug. Row 2 of Table 1 shows an example in which Dax is associated with image content and Wug with caption content. In this setting, successful performance requires the model to bind each content span to its assigned label and later retrieve the queried one, but it does not require any notion of modality. In Figure 3, Qwen2.5-VL-32B and Gemma-3-12B perform nearly perfectly under this task. Although InternVL3-14B performs worse than the other two models, it still succeeds well above chance. These results show that VLMs are capable of using arbitrary symbols as indexing devices, just like their language model counterparts.

3.2 VLMs Encode Tokens of Different Modalities in a Linearly Separable Manner

A second potential source of distinction comes from the distributional properties of image and text token representations. Here, we ask whether these representations are already separable before any contextual processing by the language model. Therefore, we examine them at the embedding layer of the backbone language model. To do so, we sample 200 instances from a dataset and, for each instance, sample the embedding representation of one token from each modality. We then measure cosine similarity between embedding pairs within and across modalities, and also train a linear probe to distinguish image-token representations from text-token representations. To evaluate linear separability, we use stratified 3-fold cross-validation.

Across all model-dataset pairs, we find that the averaged within-modality cosine similarity (0.21±0.060.21\pm 0.06) is substantially higher than cross-modality cosine similarity (0.02±0.020.02\pm 0.02). This suggests that tokens from the same modality are more similar to one another than to tokens from the other modality. Consistent with this, a linear probe can separate image and caption tokens with perfect cross-validation accuracy across all models and datasets we test, indicating that image and text representations are linearly separable to a very high degree.44 4 See detailed results in Table 4 in the appendix.

3.3 Structural Perturbation on Symbolic Markers

Next, we study how symbolic and distributional signals each or together affect VLMs’ ability to monitor source modalities, and retrieve from the target modality. To approach this, we systematically perturb the symbolic marker tokens by removing them or swapping them across modalities (see row 3 and 4 in Table 1). If the model uses a purely symbolic mechanism, we would expect to see a performance near chance when symbolic markers are removed, and models’ predictions completely reversed when they are swapped; on the other hand, if the model relies solely on the distributional signals, we would expect these perturbations to have minimal effects on models’ performance.

Figure 4 shows the result of swapping and removing symbolic marker tokens on models’ performance in the target modality retrieval task. The aggregated results (subplots 3-5) shows that while removing marker tokens significantly reduces models’ selectivity, it does not drop towards near-zero level, which indicates VLMs are able to use the residual signals within the distributions of image/text tokens to tell a difference between modalities. Moreover, swapping the marker tokens does not reverse models’ predictions, rather it remains positive well above chance, which emphasizes that when symbolic and distributional signals conflict with each other, the model relies on the distributional signals more.

We also include results broken down by target modality in subplots 6–8 of Figure 4. We find that accuracy for reporting image content remains high across perturbation conditions, whereas accuracy for reporting caption content falls to near chance level (and even below chance for InternVL3). This sharp asymmetry suggests that VLMs learn a particularly robust way of associating the concept of “image” with image tokens, while relying more heavily on symbolic cues when retrieving caption information.

One plausible reason for the asymmetry noted above is that caption tokens are embedded among other textual spans in the input, so there is nothing about them that makes them inherently “caption” in the way image tokens are inherently “image.” We follow up on this intuition by varying the word used to refer to the caption, and observing the effect on the above trends. In this experiment, the text source is labeled as either caption, text, or document, and the query correspondingly asks what is in the image, caption, text, or document.

The results are shown in Figure 5. Models achieve high selectivity in the unperturbed condition, showing that they can reliably retrieve information from the queried source when the source markers are present. The key difference emerges under marker perturbations, which reveal that the model relies heavily on symbolic marker tokens when the text is referred to as the document, and relies on them very little when it is referred to as text. This suggests an interesting and intuitive mechanism, in which models encode a notion of the type of input that is typically referred to by specific words. That is, the model is happy to bind the word text to text in the prompt, whether or not that text is prefixed with a marker such as “Text:”. In contrast, the model is resistant to considering an arbitrary short piece of text to be a document unless it is explicitly labeled as such.55 5 One plausible reason is that the category document is intrinsically less distributionally distinct from images than text: documents can contain heterogeneous content, including embedded images, and therefore may provide a weaker standalone signal of source identity.

3.4 Propagation of Symbolic Signals onto Content Tokens

In this subsection, we investigate how symbolic and distributional signals interact, focusing on whether symbolic marker tokens help write modality identity information into content-token representations. Our hypothesis is that this happens through contextualization across layers: marker tokens influence the hidden states of downstream content tokens, causing modality identity to become embedded in those representations rather than remaining localized at the marker positions.

To isolate this effect, we first run the model on the normal input with intact markers and collect the hidden activations at the content-token positions after they have been contextualized in the presence of those markers. We then perform a second run in which the marker tokens are removed, but the contextualized content-token activations from the clean run are patched in and frozen (Figure 11). We refer to this intervention as the freeze-remove condition (Frz-RM).

Figure 6 shows that symbolic information does not remain confined to the marker positions. In the Frz-RM condition, selectivity is partially restored relative to conditions in which markers are removed from the outset. This suggests that, during contextualization, information carried by the marker tokens is propagated into downstream content-token representations. Once contextualized in this way, content tokens encode not only their native distributional signals, but also the signal of modality identity inherited from the symbolic markers.

The modality-specific breakdown further shows that both image and caption content benefit from this contextualization, though the gain is much larger for caption content. For Gemma-3-12B and Qwen2.5-VL-32B, caption-target selectivity rises from near chance to around 0.6 under Frz-RM. For InternVL3-14B, the effect is weaker, but still mitigates the negative selectivity observed when markers are removed without using the contextualized activations. These results suggest that symbolic markers become more effective not only as explicit tokens, but also by shaping the representations of downstream content tokens.

4 Robustness of Symbolic vs Distributional Signals of Modality

4.1 Experiment Setup

We have shown that VLMs rely on both symbolic signals from marker tokens and distributional signals from content tokens to monitor input modalities, we now ask whether these signals can be manipulated to induce misattribution. Specifically, we study a setting in which we add two learned vectors, δ1\delta_{1} and δ2\delta_{2}, to the image span and caption span, respectively (Figure 7), either at the marker positions or at the content-token positions at a specific layer. We then prompt the model to report, for example, the image content, but optimize these vectors to make the model instead produce the caption content, using the model’s own caption-side prediction from a natural run as the target; symmetrically, we also optimize in the reverse direction, asking for caption content while driving the model toward its natural image-side prediction. If these marker and content representations indeed support source-modality monitoring, then there should exist transformations of them that systematically induce source misattribution. We initialize both δ\delta vectors to zero and train them on 4,000 samples from the training split of MSCOCO. For each model, we optimize them at various relative layer depths and we repeat the procedure across 3 random seeds.

4.2 Results

Figure 8 shows the selectivity of Qwen2.5-VL-32B after applying learned δ\delta vectors to either content spans or marker spans at different relative layer depths, evaluated on 100 validation examples unseen during training. In early and middle layers, interventions on both content and marker representations can drive the model to systematically report the opposite modality of the target modality. This effect is especially strong for marker-token interventions, which achieve selectivities close to -1 across a broad range of layers.

Notably, these learned interventions are substantially more effective than the marker-swapping manipulation presented earlier in the paper. This suggests that learned transformation vectors exploit modality-relevant information in marker representations more effectively than a simple symbolic swap. While both can influence how modality identity is propagated into downstream content representations, the learned vectors are optimized for this purpose and thus more successfully override native distributional cues.

The intervention effect weakens in later layers for both marker and content locations. This suggests that the representations supporting source-modality monitoring are most causally relevant in early and middle layers, and become harder to exploit after later-stage processing has already built on them. Taken together, these results show that both marker and content representations are represented as subspaces which can be steered, but that the marker-tokens provide a particularly strong causal handle for accessing this subspace.66 6 See qualitative examples of VLMs’ predictions being flipped after intervention in Appendix J.2.

5 Related Work

Cross-Modal Conflict in VLMs

Prior work has used inconsistent multimodal inputs to study modality bias in VLM predictions (Deng et al., 2025; Pezeshkpour et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). While these studies show that VLMs can favor one modality over another depending on the model, dataset, or relative unimodal confidence, they typically use questions that remain ambiguously answerable from either modality, or focus mainly on the image side of the conflict. More closely related to our setting, Hua et al. (2025) explicitly query both image and caption information under inconsistent inputs. Our work broadens the evaluation from their setup to more VLMs across scales and model families, and studies the underlying signals which enables VLMs to accomplish this task.

Structural Perturbations on Special Tokens

Shayegani et al. (2025) shows that perturbing assistant and user role tags or placing query images under the assistant turn can induce misaligned behaviors in vision-language models. Similarly, we study structural perturbations but on special tokens related to the modality structure: we manipulate the image start and end tokens to probe how symbolic modality markers support source-modality monitoring.

6 Discussion and Conclusion

We investigate the mechanism by which modern VLMs bind words in their input prompts (e.g., words like image or text) to specific components of their input/context (e.g., the image or the text). In experiments spanning 11 different vision-language models (VLMs), we find evidence that this type of binding involves both syntactic and semantic signals. That is, models exploit explicit marker tokens (such as <image> & </image>) when available, but also exploit distributional semantic cues. Indeed, we find that when the two signals are in conflict, models rely more on the distributional semantic cues than on the syntactic ones, though this varies as a function of the strength of the distributional signal.

Our experiments focus specifically on VLMs, but offer insights that are likely to extend to multimodal and agentic models in general. In particular, as models become increasingly complex, multimodal, and agentic, we expect that the importance of semantic signals for binding will become increasingly pronounced. This is due to the fact that models appear to have an innate preference for distributional semantic signals (when both signals are available), and because it will become increasingly impractical to provide explicit markers as the complexity of the input space grows. Indeed, our results comparing the different in binding the words text vs. caption vs. document reveal the challenge of grounding references to “micromodalities” – segments of the input space that are different enough to humans to warrant different words, but which might be hard to distinguish to the model based on distributional signals alone. These point to an important direction for future work – to endow models with rich enough world models that they can not only predict future states, but refer back to aspects of those states and their origin via natural language.

Our results also provide a valuable case study for how the abstract “binding problem” in AI becomes more complicated in realistic contexts. Binding has frequently been used as an example of an abstract symbolic problem that challenges the innate tendencies of neural networks. The type of binding we consider, that necessary for source-modality monitoring, represents a more realistic type of binding which involves both abstract symbolic and associative semantic signals. Our experiments provide an initial picture of how these signals are traded off within modern AI models, and provide a framework for investigating similar mechanisms in general, for example considering how models balance logical and heuristic inferences (Dasgupta et al., 2024).

Appendix A Dataset Details

We use two image–captioning datasets: MSCOCO 2017 captions and Flickr30k.

Flickr30k.

For Flickr30k, we use the test split from the lmms-lab/flickr30k release on HuggingFace. We then randomly permute the examples using a fixed seed and subsample 4,000 examples for train, 2,000 for validation, and 2,000 for test.

MSCOCO.

For MSCOCO, we use the 2017 captioning data. We sample the training set from the official train2017 split, and the validation and test sets from the official val2017 split. Specifically, after randomly permuting examples with a fixed seed, we sample 4,000 examples from train2017 for train, and 2,000 examples each from val2017 for validation and test.

Preprocessing.

We lightly normalize captions before use by collapsing repeated whitespace, stripping surrounding quotation marks, and ensuring sentence-final punctuation when appropriate. These steps reduce superficial formatting variation while preserving semantic content.

Use in our experiments.

Both datasets are used to construct the image–text inputs in our source-modality monitoring task. Because each image is paired with textual descriptions, these datasets allow us to build inconsistent image–text examples, as well as image-only and text-only controls.

Appendix B Measuring Valid Response Rate and Selectivity

We evaluate source-modality monitoring with two separate metrics: valid-response rate (pvalidp_{\mathrm{valid}}) and selectivity. Intuitively, pvalidp_{\mathrm{valid}} measures whether the model gives an on-task response that can be attributed to one of the two candidate modalities, while selectivity measures, among such valid responses, whether the model reports information from the requested modality rather than the non-requested one.

Formally, let y^i\hat{y}_{i} denote the model output for example ii, and let the queried modality be m∈{image,caption}m\in\{\text{image},\text{caption}\}, with the other modality denoted ¬m\neg m. For each modality, define a modality-assignment indicator

Mi(m)​(y^i)∈{0,1},M_{i}^{(m)}(\hat{y}_{i})\in\{0,1\},

which equals 11 if the output is judged to be grounded in modality mm, and 00 otherwise. Likewise, Mi(¬m)​(y^i)M_{i}^{(\neg m)}(\hat{y}_{i}) indicates whether the output is judged to be grounded in the non-queried modality. We use GPT5.4-mini as an LLM judge to decide whether a piece of response is grounded in image, in caption, or in neither.

We define a response to be valid if it is an on-task answer that the judge assigns to any one of the two modalities. This gives the binary indicator

valid⁡(y^i)=Mi(m)​(y^i)+Mi(¬m)​(y^i).\mathrm{valid}(\hat{y}_{i})=M_{i}^{(m)}(\hat{y}_{i})+M_{i}^{(\neg m)}(\hat{y}_{i}).

The valid-response rate is then

pvalid=𝔼⁡[valid⁡(y^)].p_{\mathrm{valid}}=\mathbb{E}\big[\mathrm{valid}(\hat{y})\big].

We define selectivity as the tendency, among valid responses, to report information from the queried modality rather than the non-queried modality:

S=𝔼⁡[M(m)​(y^)−M(¬m)​(y^)|valid⁡(y^)=1].S=\mathbb{E}\Big[M^{(m)}(\hat{y})-M^{(\neg m)}(\hat{y})\;\Big|\;\mathrm{valid}(\hat{y})=1\Big].

This score ranges from −1-1 to 11: a value of 11 indicates that all valid responses are grounded in the queried modality, a value of 00 indicates no preference between the two modalities, and a value of −1-1 indicates that all valid responses are grounded in the non-queried modality.

Appendix C Input and Query Prompt Templates for VLMs

Our prompt templates vary along two controlled dimensions: (1) the order in which the image and caption inputs appear, and (2) the surface form used to query the target modality. For source order, we evaluate both image-first and caption-first variants. For query wording, we use two formulations for each modality: for image queries, What is in the image? and Describe the image.; for caption queries, What is in the caption? and What does the caption say? Table 2 summarizes these variations, and Figure 9 shows one representative raw prompt including the model-specific chat template and special image tokens.

Appendix H Experimental Setup for the Freeze-Remove Condition

Figure 11 shows an illustration of the freeze-remove experiment condition. We collect activations from a clean run (with the marker tokens intact), and then patch these collected activations into a corrupt run where the marker tokens are removed – we then allow any downstream computation to continue based on the patched-in activations. This allows us to study the effect of contextualization of content tokens in source-modality monitoring.

Appendix I Additional Results for Comparing Alternative Source-Modality Pairs

J.2 Qualitative Examples

We notice that after intervention, although in some settings VLMs often report information from the non-queried modality, the overall fluency of the open-ended generation degrades. This is likely because the intervention perturbs representations that are used not only for source-modality monitoring but also for maintaining coherent generation.
